Leadership Beyond Titles: 10 Lessons from AYF Canada

A reflection on leadership, responsibility, organizational life, and service

Moses Arzomanian · July 2026 · 10 min read

After years of service with AYF Canada, I look back on a chapter that contributed greatly to my understanding of leadership, responsibility, service, and organizational life.

My experience with AYF Canada was not only about holding responsibilities, participating in meetings, organizing initiatives, or working with volunteers. It was also a long process of learning how organizations function, how people respond to leadership, how decisions create consequences, and how values are tested when circumstances become difficult.

Looking back, some of the most important lessons I learned did not come from moments of success alone. Many came from difficult conversations, unresolved challenges, mistakes, disagreements, changing circumstances, and the responsibility of making decisions that affected others.

These are ten leadership lessons that will continue to influence the way I approach leadership, education, organizational development, and service.

• • •

Lesson 1
Pragmatism Is Justified Only When It Does Not Compromise Core Principles

Leadership often requires practical decisions. Circumstances change, resources may be limited, and leaders frequently need to adapt their approach to reality. Pragmatism is therefore necessary.

However, practicality should never come at the expense of the principles and identity that define an organization.

There is a difference between adapting the method and abandoning the purpose. An organization can change how it works, modernize its processes, and respond to new realities while remaining faithful to the values that justify its existence in the first place.

For me, this became one of the clearest tests of leadership: knowing when compromise is a reasonable adjustment and when it begins to undermine the organization's core ideology.

Lesson 2
Unresolved Problems Should Not Be Ignored

One of the easiest mistakes in organizational life is assuming that a problem will disappear if enough time passes.

Usually, it does not.

Unresolved problems tend to return in more complicated forms. Small misunderstandings can become larger conflicts, unclear responsibilities can create frustration, and issues that could have been addressed early can eventually affect an entire team.

Healthy organizations need the courage to identify problems, discuss them openly, and address them constructively.

This does not mean reacting impulsively to every difficulty. It means refusing to confuse avoidance with patience. Sometimes leadership requires allowing time for reflection, but there is an important difference between taking time to understand an issue and simply postponing it because the conversation is uncomfortable.

Lesson 3
Knowledge Should Be Discovered, Not Merely Dictated

One of the most important lessons I learned through educational and leadership work is that people rarely develop strong convictions simply because someone tells them what to believe.

Meaningful learning happens when individuals are encouraged to think critically, ask questions, explore different perspectives, and arrive at conclusions through reflection and experience.

This principle applies far beyond the classroom.

In organizations, especially those working with young people, leadership should not only provide answers. It should create environments in which people learn how to think.

A strong educational process does not produce people who simply repeat what they were told. It develops individuals who understand why they believe something, can defend their ideas thoughtfully, and are willing to reconsider them when presented with better reasoning.

Leadership and education became increasingly connected through this principle: create environments where people learn how to think, not just what to think.

Lesson 4
Talent Management Is a Central Responsibility of Leadership

Organizations are often full of capable people whose potential is never fully developed.

Good leadership is not simply about identifying the most talented individuals. It is about understanding people well enough to recognize their strengths, help them improve, and place them in roles where those strengths can serve the organization effectively.

Not everyone needs to lead in the same way. Some people are strong organizers. Others are excellent communicators. Some work best behind the scenes. Others thrive in public-facing roles. Some need more guidance before taking responsibility, while others need space and trust.

When people are placed in the wrong roles, both the individual and the organization can suffer. When their strengths are recognized and developed, they often contribute far more than they initially believed they could.

Talent management, therefore, is not secondary to leadership. It is one of its central responsibilities.

Lesson 5
Integrity Is More Important Than Position

Positions change. Titles end. Circumstances evolve.

Integrity remains.

Leadership can sometimes create an unhealthy attachment to titles, authority, or recognition. But a position does not define a leader's character. The real test comes when there is something to lose.

Remaining faithful to one's principles when doing so is convenient is relatively easy. Remaining faithful to them when circumstances become difficult is what gives those principles meaning.

Over time, I came to believe that credibility is built less through the title someone holds and more through consistency between what they say, what they believe, and how they act. A leadership position may last for a year or several years. Reputation and character remain much longer.

Lesson 6
Success Should Not Be Measured Only by Financial Achievement

Organizations naturally need financial stability. Budgets matter, fundraising matters, and resources are necessary to turn ideas into action.

But financial achievement alone cannot be the definition of success.

An organization may raise significant amounts of money and still fail in its mission. A project may produce impressive numbers while damaging relationships, values, or institutional trust.

Leadership therefore requires a broader understanding of achievement. Success should also include the quality of the work accomplished, the people developed through the process, the values preserved, and the ability to look back on a decision with a clear conscience.

There are moments when the most financially advantageous decision may not be the decision that best reflects the organization's values. Leaders need to be able to distinguish between the two.

Lesson 7
Help Is Most Effective When Someone Is Ready to Receive It

Leadership often creates a strong desire to help people. But help cannot always be imposed.

There are moments when someone may not yet recognize a problem, may not be prepared to receive guidance, or may interpret assistance as interference.

Sometimes the role of a leader is not to solve someone's problem immediately. It is to create the conditions in which that individual can eventually recognize the need for support and feel comfortable asking for it.

Guidance becomes much more effective when there is openness on both sides. This does not mean leaders should ignore people who are struggling. It means understanding that timing, trust, and readiness are often part of the helping process.

Lesson 8
Courage Includes the Ability to Live with Failure

Leadership is often associated with confidence, decisive action, and success. But courage also includes the ability to accept failure.

Anyone who takes responsibility will eventually make mistakes. Projects will fail. Decisions will produce unexpected consequences. People will sometimes disappoint us, and we will sometimes disappoint ourselves.

The goal cannot be to build a leadership career without failure. The goal is to develop the maturity to face failure honestly, understand what happened, learn from it, and continue forward.

Responsible leadership requires enough courage to act, enough humility to recognize mistakes, and enough resilience to continue learning afterward.

Lesson 9
Comfort Can Become Dangerous for an Organization

Organizations naturally seek stability. Stability can be healthy — it allows systems to develop, people to understand their responsibilities, and institutions to preserve continuity.

But excessive comfort can become dangerous.

When an organization becomes too comfortable, it may stop questioning itself. Practices may continue simply because they have always existed. Innovation slows. Responsible risks become less attractive. Challenges may be minimized because confronting them would disrupt familiar routines.

Long-term relevance requires continuous reflection and renewal. Organizations need to ask whether their methods are still serving their mission, whether new generations are being prepared effectively, and whether old structures remain appropriate for current realities.

Respecting tradition does not mean resisting improvement. Healthy institutions preserve what is essential while remaining willing to change what no longer serves the purpose.

Lesson 10
Bylaws and Institutional Rules Matter

Strong organizations cannot depend entirely on personalities.

Charismatic leaders can inspire people and move projects forward, but institutions need systems that continue functioning regardless of who happens to be in charge. Bylaws, clearly defined responsibilities, procedures, accountability mechanisms, and consistent rules are therefore essential.

When structures are unclear, decisions can become personal. Expectations change depending on the people involved, accountability becomes inconsistent, and institutional memory weakens.

Rules should not exist simply for bureaucracy. Their purpose is to protect fairness, continuity, transparency, and the organization itself.

The goal is not to build an organization around individuals. It is to build an institution strong enough to continue serving its mission across generations.

Leadership Lessons That Continue Beyond a Position

These ten lessons will continue to influence the way I think about leadership, education, organizational development, responsibility, and service.

My experience with AYF Canada gave me opportunities to lead, teach, organize, learn from others, make mistakes, reconsider assumptions, and better understand the responsibility that comes with organizational life.

I am sincerely grateful to everyone who contributed to that experience. Some shared their knowledge and perspectives with me. Others challenged my thinking, disagreed with me, trusted me with responsibility, or helped create situations from which important lessons emerged. All of these experiences contributed to my growth.

Leadership development is rarely the result of one person teaching another exactly what to do. It is built gradually through relationships, responsibilities, successes, failures, reflection, and experience.

As this chapter ends, I am confident that new generations will continue the path. They will inherit both the achievements and the mistakes of those who came before them. Their responsibility will not be simply to repeat what previous generations did, but to understand it, learn from it, improve upon it, and carry the mission further.

That is ultimately how healthy organizations survive.

Some of the most valuable lessons are not the ones we simply remember. They are the ones that gradually become part of the way we lead, the way we make decisions, and the way we live.
